Respondent by: Mr. Mohsin Khan, Advocate.

body: CONSOLIDATED JUDGMENT *** MUHAMMAD FAHEEM WALI, J.‐ Through this single judgment, I propose to decide the instant civil revision as well as the connected C.R. No. 877-P/2025, as both the petitions are directed against one and the same order dated 08.03.2025 passed by the learned Additional District Judge- I, Shabqadar, District Charsadda, in Civil Suit No. 01/1 of 2024, whereby the written statement of Amir Ilyas (defendant No. 2) was discarded for want of an application for leave to defend and the plaintiff, Malik Gohar Ali, was directed to produce his evidence. Amir Ilyas has assailed the order to the extent of discarding of his written statement, whereas Malik Gohar Ali has assailed it to the extent of the direction to produce evidence instead of passing a decree under Order XXXVII Rule 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC). As the parties are arrayed differently in the two petitions, they shall, for the sake of
(2) convenience, be referred to by their status in the suit, i.e. Malik Gohar Ali as the plaintiff, Rahman Ullah as defendant No. 1 and Amir Ilyas as defendant No. 2.

2. Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the instant petitions are that the plaintiff instituted a suit under Order XXXVII CPC against the defendants for recovery of Rs. 50,00,000/- along with interest under sections 79 and 80 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (the Act of 1881), and a further sum of Rs. 25,00,000/- as special damages. It was averred in the plaint that defendant No. 1 had obtained a loan of Rs. 50,00,000/- from the plaintiff vide agreement deed No. 35 dated 23.08.2022, repayable within three months, and, for the said purpose, handed over cheque No. 2466256281 drawn on his account with Allied Bank; that the cheque was delivered through defendant No. 2, who stood surety for repayment of the loan; that on default the defendants promised to pay by 01.04.2023, when defendant No. 2 again stood surety; and that on presentation the cheque was dishonoured for insufficient funds, whereafter FIR No. 929 dated 12.10.2023 under sections 489-F/420 PPC was registered at Police Station Shabqadar.

3. Defendant No. 2, after service of summons on 31.05.2024, appeared through counsel and on 08.06.2024 submitted a written statement instead of an application for leave to defend, wherein he denied any concern with the transaction, asserted that he had signed the deed merely as a marginal witness and never as surety, that he was not a signatory to the cheque, and that the word “surety” had subsequently been inserted in the deed. Defendant No. 1, despite service through registered post, did not appear and

(3) was proceeded against ex‐parte on 19.12.2024. The learned trial Court, which had described the written statement of defendant No. 2 in its order dated 25.07.2024 as an “application for leave to defend/written statement”, fixed the case for arguments on leave to defend on several dates and, after hearing arguments, passed the impugned order, whereby the written statement of defendant No. 2 was discarded for want of an application for leave to defend and the plaintiff was directed to produce his entire evidence on the ground that “the huge amount is involved”.

4. Defendant No. 2 assailed the said order through C.R. No. 407-P/2025. Vide order dated 09.04.2025, this Court issued pre-admission notice to the plaintiff and suspended the proceedings before the learned trial Court, whereafter, on 14.04.2025, the learned trial Court adjourned the suit sine die till the disposal of the revision petition. The plaintiff, on the other hand, filed C.R. No. 877- P/2025 on 21.06.2025, along with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 for condonation of delay.

5. Learned counsel for defendant No. 2 (petitioner in C.R. No. 407-P/2025) contended that his client is neither the drawer nor an endorser of the cheque and, in view of section 29A of the Act of 1881, cannot be held liable thereon; that the claim against him, if any, rests on an alleged contract of guarantee under section 126 of the Contract Act, 1872 (Contract Act), which being a general law cannot be enforced through the special procedure meant only for negotiable instruments; that the written statement was filed within ten days of service, disclosed a

(4) bona fide defence, was received on record without objection and was treated by the learned trial Court itself as an application for leave to defend, therefore, it could not be discarded on a mere technicality; and that the impugned order has deprived his client of the right to fair trial guaranteed under Article 10-A of the Constitution.

6. Conversely, learned counsel for the plaintiff (petitioner in C.R. No. 877-P/2025) contended that in summary suits the procedural timelines are mandatory; that the learned trial Court rightly discarded the written statement of defendant No. 2 for want of a formal application for leave to defend supported by affidavit; that once the defence was discarded and defendant No. 1 had been proceeded against ex‐parte, the allegations in the plaint stood admitted and the learned trial Court was bound to pass a decree under Order XXXVII Rule 2(2) CPC; that the direction to produce evidence converts a summary suit into an ordinary one and defeats the very object of Order XXXVII CPC; and that defendant No. 2, having stood surety for defendant No. 1, became immediately liable under section 126 of the Contract Act on the default of the principal debtor. He prayed that this Court may itself pass a decree for Rs. 50,00,000/- with interest as well as special damages. As regards limitation, he submitted that the delay was neither deliberate nor mala fide, the plaintiff being under the bona fide impression that the impugned order was partly in his favour, and that the same order was already under challenge before this Court in the connected revision.
7. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with their able assistance.

(5) 8. First, the question of limitation in C.R. No. 877- P/2025. The impugned order was passed on 08.03.2025 and the revision was filed on 21.06.2025, beyond the period of ninety days provided under section 115 CPC, by about fifteen days. The delay is not inordinate. More importantly, the legality of the very same order was already under examination by this Court in C.R. No. 407-P/2025, in which the proceedings before the learned trial Court stood suspended since 09.04.2025; the plaintiff, therefore, gained nothing by the delay and defendant No. 2 has suffered no prejudice on account of it. Even otherwise, this Court, once seized of the legality of an order under section 115 CPC, is competent to examine it in its entirety and to pass such order as it thinks fit. The delay is, therefore, condoned and the application C.M. No.1276-P/2025 is allowed.

9. Coming to the merits, the plaintiff has combined in a single plaint three distinct claims: first, a claim on the dishonoured cheque against its drawer, defendant No. 1; second, a claim against defendant No. 2, who has not signed the cheque but is alleged to have stood surety for the debt; and third, a claim for unliquidated damages. The learned trial Court dealt with all three alike. The real question that falls for determination is whether a person who has not signed a negotiable instrument can be proceeded against under the summary procedure of Order XXXVII CPC on the strength of an alleged guarantee falling under section 126 of the Contract Act, and, consequently, whether the plaintiff was entitled to a decree under Rule 2(2) of the said Order against either of the defendants. The answer lies in the
(6) interplay of section 29A of the Act of 1881, section 126 of the Contract Act, and Order XXXVII CPC.
10. For ready reference, the relevant provisions of Order XXXVII CPC are reproduced below:
“1. This Order shall apply only to the High Courts, to the District Courts and to any other Civil Court notified in this behalf by the High Court.

2. (1) All suits upon bills of exchange, hundies or promissory notes, may, in case the plaintiff desires to proceed hereunder, be instituted by presenting a plaint in the form prescribed; but the summons shall be in Form No. 4 in Appendix B or in such other form as may be from time to time prescribed.

(2) In any case in which the plaint and summons are in such forms, respectively, the defendant shall not appear or defend the suit unless he obtains leave from a Judge as hereinafter provided so to appear and defend; and, in default of his obtaining such leave or of his appearance and defence in pursuance thereof, the allegations in the plaint shall be deemed to be admitted, and the plaintiff shall be entitled to a decree— (a) for the principal sum due on the instrument and for interest calculated in accordance with the provisions of section 79 or section 80, as the case may be, of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, up to the date of the institution of the suit, or for the sum mentioned in the summons, whichever is less, and for interest up to the date of the decree at the same rate or at such other rate as the Court thinks fit;

(b) for such subsequent interest, if any, as the Court may order under section 34 of this Code; and (c) for such sum for costs as may be prescribed … (3) A decree passed under this rule may be executed forthwith.

3. (1) The Court shall, upon application by the defendant, give leave to appear and to defend the suit, upon affidavits which disclose such facts as would make it incumbent on the holder to prove consideration, or such other facts as the Court may deem sufficient to support the application. (2) Leave to defend may be given unconditionally or subject to such terms as to payment into Court, giving security, framing and recording issues or otherwise as the Court thinks fit.
(7) (3) The provisions of section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 (IX of 1908), shall apply to applications under sub-rule (1).”

11. A bare reading of the above provisions shows that every limb of the Order revolves around the instrument. The suit must be one “upon” a bill of exchange, hundi or promissory note; the deemed admission culminates in a decree for “the principal sum due on the instrument” with interest under sections 79 and 80 of the Act of 1881; and leave is to be granted on facts which would make it incumbent on “the holder” to prove consideration, which is an echo of the presumption under section 118 of the Act of 1881 operating between the parties to the instrument. Order XXXVII CPC is, thus, the procedural arm of the Act of 1881 and not a general procedure for recovery of debts. The scope of the summary procedure is, therefore, to be determined by reference to the liability which the Act of 1881 creates.

12. The Act of 1881 is a special law. Section 1A thereof ordains that every negotiable instrument shall be governed by the provisions of the Act. A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker (section 6), and a bill of exchange is, by definition, an instrument in writing “signed by the maker” (section 5). Sections 26 to 29C then lay down, as a self-contained code, who may be bound by an instrument and how. The provisions germane to the controversy are reproduced below:
“26. Every person capable of contracting, according to the law to which he is subject, may bind himself and be bound by the making, drawing, acceptance, endorsement,

(8) delivery and negotiation of a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque. … 27. Every person capable of binding himself or of being bound, as mentioned in section 26, may so bind himself or be bound by a duly authorized agent acting in his name. … 28. (1) Where a person signs a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque without adding to his signature words indicating that he signs it as an agent for and on behalf of a principal or in a representative character, he is personally liable thereon but the mere addition to his signature of words describing him as an agent or as filling a representative character does not exempt him from personal liability.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), any person signing a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque for and on behalf of the principal is not liable to a person who induces him to sign upon the belief that the principal alone would be held liable.] 29. A legal representative of a deceased person who signs his name to a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque is liable personally thereon unless he expressly limits his liability to the extent of the assets received by him as such. 29A. Signature essential to liability.— No person is liable as maker, drawer, endorser or acceptor of a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque who has not signed it as such:

Provided that where a person signs any such instrument in a trade or assumed name he is liable thereon as if he had signed it in his own name. 29C. A person placing his signature upon a negotiable instrument otherwise than as maker, drawer or acceptor is pre-sumed to be an indorser unless he clearly indicates by appropriate words his intention to be bound in some other capacity.] 37. The maker of a promissory note or cheque, the drawer of a bill of exchange until acceptance, and the acceptor are, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, respectively liable thereon as principal debtors, and the other parties thereto are liable thereon as sureties for the maker, drawer or acceptor, as the case may be.”

13. The thread running through these provisions is unmistakable: every liability which the Act of 1881 creates is tied to a signature placed on the instrument in a given capacity. Even an agent, a legal representative or a stranger

(9) is bound only because he has signed. Section 29A puts the matter beyond doubt by declaring, in negative terms, that no person is liable as maker, drawer, endorser or acceptor of a cheque who has not signed it as such. Likewise, the “sureties” contemplated by section 37 are “the other parties thereto”, i.e. persons whose names stand on the instrument, such as endorsers.

14. The liability of a guarantor, on the other hand, springs from the Contract Act, which is the general law of obligations. Sections 126 and 128 thereof read as under: “126. A “contract of guarantee” is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives the guarantee is called the “surety”; the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given is called the “principal debtor”, and the person to whom the guarantee is given is called the “creditor”. A guarantee may be either oral or written.
128. The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract.”

15. A contract of guarantee is, thus, a distinct and collateral contract, which may even be oral, and whose existence, terms and consideration (section 127) are matters of proof. Section 1 of the Contract Act itself saves the provisions of other enactments not expressly repealed.
16. Adverting to the case in hand, cheque No.

2466256281 is drawn by defendant No. 1 on his own account, payable to the plaintiff or bearer, and bears the signature of defendant No. 1 alone. It is nowhere the case of the plaintiff that defendant No. 2 signed the cheque as drawer, endorser or in any other capacity; the highest that is pleaded is that the cheque was handed over “through”

(10) him. Mere delivery of an instrument signed by another does not make the person delivering it a party thereto. Defendant No. 2, therefore, is not liable on the cheque by virtue of the express bar contained in section 29A of the Act of 1881, and section 29C does not come into play as he has not signed the instrument at all. The observation of the learned trial Court that defendant No. 2 had “admitted the issuance of cheque” is a clear misreading of the record, as he never issued any cheque and, on the contrary, specifically denied any concern with it.

17. Nor can defendant No. 2 be termed a “surety” within the meaning of section 37 of the Act of 1881, which, as noticed above, refers to parties whose names stand on the instrument. A person who undertakes, outside the instrument, to pay in case the drawer defaults is a surety only in the sense of section 126 of the Contract Act. Stripped of its label, therefore, the claim of the plaintiff against defendant No. 2 is founded on a contract of guarantee, said to be evidenced by deed No. 35 dated 23.08.2022 and a writing dated 01.04.2023. The deed has been executed between the plaintiff as first party and defendant No. 1 as second party, whereas the name of defendant No. 2 appears in its margin as a witness; and defendant No. 2 alleges that the words describing him as surety were inserted afterwards. Whether defendant No. 2 in fact undertook to discharge the liability of defendant No. 1, whether the deed was tampered with, and whether the writing dated 01.04.2023 is genuine, are all questions of fact requiring evidence, on which no opinion is being expressed by this Court.

(11) 18. Learned counsel for defendant No. 2 has rightly characterised the Act of 1881 as a special law and the Contract Act as a general law. In fact, the two enactments operate in their own respective fields: the former governs liability on the instrument, the latter governs the collateral promise of a guarantor. The maxim generalia specialibus non derogant would, however, squarely apply if the general law were pressed into service to fasten upon a person a liability which the special law expressly excludes, and that is precisely the effect of the argument advanced on behalf of the plaintiff. No doubt, under section 128 of the Contract Act the liability of a surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor and, as held by the Supreme Court of India in Bank of Bihar Ltd. v. Damodar Prasad (AIR 1969 SC 297), is immediate; but co-extensive with the debt of the principal debtor does not mean liability on the cheque of the principal debtor. Section 128 merely measures the extent of the surety’s obligation once the guarantee is proved; it cannot make him a party to an instrument which he never signed, for that would allow the general law to override the express mandate of section 29A of the special law.

19. This view finds support from consistent judicial opinion. In Mst. Zubiada Khanam v. Haji Muhammad Siddique (PLD 2026 Lahore 716), the worthy Lahore High Court held that Section 29-A embodies the principle that liability on a negotiable instrument is confined to the person who has actually signed it and the provision reinforces the rule that responsibility attaches to the signatory alone, thereby excluding persons who have not executed the instrument. To the same effect are Bushra Bibi

(12) v. Additional District Judge (2022 CLD 900 Lahore), wherein it was held that in view of section 29A the liability is only of the maker of the cheque, and Muhammad Abaid Ullah v. Atteq‐ur‐Rehman (2015 CLC 641 Lahore), wherein it was ruled that summary suit could only be filed against the executants of bill of exchange, hundies or promissory notes and not otherwise, and party who was not a drawer or maker of a cheque/bill of exchange was not liable thereon and he could not be sued under O.XXXVII, Rr.2 & 3, C.P.C. The Supreme Court of India, in Aparna A. Shah v. Sheth Developers (P) Ltd. ((2013) 8 SCC 71), reached the same conclusion even without an equivalent of section 29A, holding that only the person who has signed the cheque can be proceeded against for its dishonour.

20. Viewed from the angle of Order XXXVII CPC, the result is the same. Rule 2(1) is confined to “suits upon bills of exchange, hundies or promissory notes”, and a suit against an alleged guarantor is a suit upon the guarantee and not upon the cheque. Rule 2(2), being penal in its effect, must be strictly construed; no sum can be said to be “due on the instrument” from a person who, under section 29A, is not liable on it. It is instructive that when the Indian legislature intended to bring guarantees within the summary procedure, it did so expressly through the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976, by inserting clause (b)(iii) in Order XXXVII Rule 1(2), covering suits “on a guarantee, where the claim against the principal is in respect of a debt or a liquidated demand only”. No such amendment has been made in Pakistan, and what the legislature has not enacted cannot be supplied by interpretation. With respect,

(13) the view taken in Habib Bank Ltd. v. Ghazangarullah Khan and another (PLD 1978 Karachi 263), to the extent it may be read as permitting summary procedure against a nonsignatory guarantor, cannot be reconciled with the plain language of section 29A and Rule 2(1). The correct course, as held in Mst. Suriya Waseem Usmani v. L & M International (Pvt.) Ltd. (2002 CLD 624) and approved in principle in Khatija Bai v. Muslim Commercial Bank (PLD 1978 SC 96), is to decide the claim on the instrument against its signatory under Order XXXVII and to try the claim against the others under the ordinary procedure.

21. It follows that, as against defendant No. 2, the suit is an ordinary suit governed by the general procedure of the CPC; the mere issuance of summons in Form No. 4 could not alter the nature of the claim against him. The deemed admission envisaged by Rule 2(2) could not operate against him, and the plaintiff was not entitled to a summary decree against him. By the same token, defendant No. 2 was under no obligation to seek leave, and his written statement dated 08.06.2024 was a written statement properly so called; its discarding by the learned trial Court was, therefore, without lawful authority.

22. Even otherwise, assuming that Order XXXVII CPC did apply to defendant No. 2, the impugned order could not be sustained, nor could the plaintiff have claimed a decree against him, as Rule 2(2) operates only in default of his obtaining such leave. Neither Rule 3 nor Form No. 4 prescribes any particular form or title for an application for leave; what is required is that the defendant, within ten days of service, seeks permission to defend on oath,

(14) disclosing facts sufficient to support his request. It is the substance and not the form which matters, as held in Zohair Akhtar v. Jawad Adil (2006 YLR 1510); and in Ghulam Hussain v. Rab Nawaz (1999 YLR 1282) the Lahore High Court deprecated the refusal of leave after a written statement had been received on record. In the present case, defendant No. 2 was served on 31.05.2024 and filed his written statement on 08.06.2024, well within time; he disclosed a specific defence; the learned trial Court itself treated the written statement as an “application for leave to defend/written statement” and fixed it for arguments as such on as many as five dates; and the plaintiff raised no objection to its form. Having so treated it for nine months, the learned trial Court could not turn round and hold that no application for leave existed.

23. The judgment in Umer Khan v. Haji Musa Jan (2009 SCMR 1101), which lays down that a written statement cannot take the place of an application for leave, may be noticed at this stage. In that case, the suit was founded on a promissory note, affidavits and an agreement executed by the defendant himself, who had admitted his signatures thereon; the trial Court had directed him to file a written statement, and it was argued before the Supreme Court that the ordinary procedure had thereby been adopted. The Supreme Court repelled the argument, holding that Order XXXVII CPC provides a special procedure for suits covered by Rule 2 and that a defendant appearing in such a suit has to seek leave by filing an application under Rule 3. The rule so laid down presupposes a defendant who is a party to the instrument and against whom the suit is,

(15) therefore, properly one under Rule 2. That is not the position of defendant No. 2, who has neither made nor signed the cheque in suit, and against whom the suit, as held above, is not one under Rule 2 at all.

24. Similarly, in Muhammad Mansab v. Muhammad Hanif (2025 SCMR 60), relied upon by the learned trial Court, the defendant had never appeared before the trial Court despite all modes of service, including substituted service; he did not apply for leave at all, and only after a decree had been passed did he move an application under Order XXXVII Rule 4 CPC to set it aside, alleging non-service. The Supreme Court held that the “special circumstances” contemplated by Rule 4 must be rare, exceptional and beyond human control, and found none, the address in the suit being the same as in his own application. The judgment, thus, concerns the setting aside of a decree passed against an absent defendant and has no bearing on a defendant who appeared within time and filed his defence in writing. On the contrary, a defendant who denies having signed the instrument raises not merely a triable issue but a complete answer to a claim on the instrument and, applying the principles laid down in Fine Textile Mills Ltd., Karachi v. Haji Umar (PLD 1963 SC 163), would in any case be entitled to unconditional leave.

25. The position of defendant No. 1, however, stands on an entirely different footing, and to this extent the grievance of the plaintiff is well-founded. Defendant No. 1 is the drawer of the cheque and, under section 37 of the Act of 1881, the principal debtor thereon; the claim against him for the cheque amount is a suit “upon” a bill of exchange

(16) within the contemplation of Rule 2(1). He neither appeared nor applied for leave and was proceeded against ex‐parte. If he was served with summons in the prescribed form and ten days elapsed without an application for leave, the allegations in the plaint were to be deemed admitted and the plaintiff became entitled to a decree for the principal sum due on the instrument with interest, as held in Naeem Iqbal v. Mst. Zarina (1996 SCMR 1530), subject only to the Court applying its mind to the plaintiff’s entitlement as required by Haji Ali Khan & Company v. M/s Allied Bank of Pakistan Ltd. (PLD 1995 SC 362). The learned trial Court did neither; it did not even advert to the claim against defendant No. 1 and directed the plaintiff to lead evidence merely because “the huge amount is involved”, a consideration alien to Order XXXVII CPC. This amounts to failure to exercise a jurisdiction vested in the Court.

26. As regards the claim for Rs. 25,00,000/- as damages for humiliation, mental torture and the like, it is neither a claim upon an instrument nor a liquidated demand, and could not be decreed under Order XXXVII CPC against either defendant. To that extent, the direction of the learned trial Court to the plaintiff to produce evidence was justified. For the same reason, the prayer of the plaintiff that this Court should itself pass a decree for the cheque amount and special damages in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction cannot be granted; the jurisdiction under section 115 CPC is corrective in nature and does not extend to decreeing claims which are yet to be proved before the Court of first instance.

(17) 27. For the reasons recorded above, C.R. No. 407- P/2025 is allowed and the impugned order dated 08.03.2025, to the extent of discarding the written statement of defendant No. 2, is set aside. C.R. No. 877- P/2025 is partly allowed; the delay in its filing is condoned and the impugned order, to the extent of directing the plaintiff to produce evidence in respect of the claim on the cheque against defendant No. 1, is set aside, while the rest of the prayers made therein are declined. The case is remanded to the learned trial Court, which shall proceed with the claim against defendant No. 1 under Order XXXVII Rule 2 CPC after satisfying itself as to his service in the prescribed form, and with the remaining claims in the suit under the ordinary procedure, in accordance with law.

28. Needless to mention that the observations made hereinabove are confined to the question of the procedure applicable to the respective claims and shall not prejudice the case of either party on merits, which the learned trial Court shall decide independently. The interim order dated 09.04.2025 passed in C.R. No. 407-P/2025 stands vacated. No order as to costs. Copy of this judgment be placed on the file of the connected C.R. No. 877-P/2025. Announced.
05.11.2026 J U D G E (SB) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Muhammad Faheem Wali.
